div.p: Background Accurate determination of H3 K27M mutation status is critical for prognosis evaluation and treatment planning in brainstem gliomas (BSGs). We developed a clinical-radiomics model integrating 11 C-methionine ( 11 C-MET) positron emission tomography (PET), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and clinical features for non-invasive, preoperative prediction of H3 K27M mutation status in BSGs.

Methods This retrospective study included 77 patients with newly diagnosed BSG who underwent preoperative 11 C-MET PET imaging and MRI. Among them, 53 had a histologically confirmed H3 K27M mutation. Patients were randomly divided into training (n = 55) and test (n = 22) cohorts. Clinical variables significantly associated with H3 K27M mutation status were used to construct a clinical model using the extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithm. Radiomics features were extracted separately from PET and MRI images to construct individual and combined models. A clinical-radiomics integrated model was then developed by combining clinical features and the radiomics model with the best predictive performance. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA).

div.head: Results
div.p: The clinical model achieved AUCs of 0.795 and 0.790 in the training and test cohorts, respectively. The combined PET-MRI radiomics model outperformed individual PET or MRI model, with AUCs of 0.876 and 0.848 in the training and test cohorts, respectively. The clinical-radiomics integrated model achieved the highest performance with AUCs of 0.886 in the training cohort and 0.876 in the test cohort. The calibration curve showed good agreement between predicted and actual outcomes, and DCA demonstrated a superior net clinical benefit of the integrated model.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Brainstem gliomas (BSGs), arising in the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata, account for 1-2% of adult and 10-20% of pediatric primary brain tumors [1,2]. A majority of BSGs harbor the H3 K27M mutation, characterized by a lysine-to-methionine substitution at position 27 on histone H3, typically involving H3F3A or HIST1H3B/C genes.

is mutation is strongly associated with aggressive tumor behavior and poor clinical outcomes [3][4][5][6][7]. Additionally, therapies targeting H3 K27M, such as histone deacetylase inhibitors (e.g., panobinostat), have shown preliminary safety and tolerability in clinical trials (e.g., NCT02717455 and NCT03566199) [8]. us, accurate determination of H3 K27M mutation status is critical for prognosis evaluation and treatment planning.

Currently, definitive diagnosis of H3 K27M mutation relies on tissue biopsy or surgical resection, which carries inherent risks due to the critical functions and anatomical complexity of the brainstem. Furthermore, spatial tumor heterogeneity may lead to sampling errors [3]. Consequently, non-invasive imaging techniques, such as advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and amino acid positron emission tomography (PET), are gaining attention as alternative tools for molecular characterization.

Advanced MRI techniques, including multi-shell diffusion imaging and diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), have demonstrated promising results in detecting the H3 K27M mutation, especially in pediatric cohorts [9,10]. Moreover, amide proton transfer-weighted (APT-w) imaging, which reflects tissue protein and polypeptide concentrations, has shown potential in identifying H3 K27M-mutant BSGs [11]. However, their routine clinical implementation remains limited due to susceptibility to artifacts-particularly in the brainstem-and reliance on specialized acquisition protocols and complex postprocessing pipelines. In contrast, amino acid PET using tracers such as 11 C-methionine ( 11 C-MET) and 18 F-dihydroxyphenylalanine ( 18 F-DOPA) offers a more robust and clinically applicable approach. ese tracers provide quantitative information on amino acid transport activity and have been effective in glioma grading and molecular typing [12,13]. A recent study has shown that H3 K27Mmutant diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPGs) exhibited higher 11 C-MET PET semi-quantitative metrics than H3 K27M-wildtype tumors [14]. Similarly, another study has demonstrated that H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline gliomas showed significantly elevated 18 F-DOPA uptake compared to their wildtype counterparts [15]. However, these findings were derived from relatively small BSG cohorts with well-defined molecular mutation status and require further validation.

Radiomics, which extracts high-throughput quantitative features from medical images, offers a novel, noninvasive approach to reveal tumor characteristics beyond visual assessment. MRI-derived radiomics models have shown good performance in predicting H3K27M mutation status in BSGs [11,16]. PET-based radiomics has shown potential for evaluating some biomarkers of glioma, such as IDH genotype and MGMT methylation status [17][18][19][20]. However, the application of PET-derived radiomics to the assessment of H3 K27M mutation remains underexplored. Furthermore, few studies have investigated the integration of PET and MRI radiomics to improve molecular diagnostic accuracy in BSGs.

Building on the background outlined above, two questions remain unresolved: (i) whether integrating 11 C-MET PET radiomics with MRI radiomics yields measurable gains for H3 K27M stratification in BSGs, and (ii) whether routinely available clinical features provide additional incremental value. Here, we develop a multimodal radiomics model that fuses 11 C-MET PET and MRI features to jointly capture metabolic and structural tumor characteristics and systematically assess the contribution of clinical features to model performance. To our knowledge, this is the first application of 11 C-MET PET-based radiomics for H3 K27M prediction in BSGs, aiming to deliver a comprehensive, non-invasive tool for preoperative molecular diagnosis.

div.head: Patient selection
div.p: is retrospective study included patients with BSGs who underwent preoperative 11 C-MET PET and MRI at Beijing Tiantan Hospital between August 2015 and August 2024. Inclusion criteria were: (1) histologically confirmed BSG with documented H3 K27M mutation status via immunohistochemistry and/or gene sequencing; (2) no prior treatment, including surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy; and (3) availability of both 11 C-MET PET/ computed tomography (CT) and MRI acquired within two weeks, or simultaneous PET/MRI scans. Exclusion criteria were: (1) hypo-or iso-metabolic tumors on 11 C-MET PET by visual assessment and (2) poor image quality. A total of 77 patients (38 males, 39 females; mean age 12.8 ± 11.4 years, range 2-63 years) were enrolled. Of these, 53 patients had H3 K27M-mutant tumors, and 24 had wildtype tumors, with a mutation prevalence of 68.8%. According to the 2016 WHO classification of central nervous system tumors [21], the cohort comprised 6, 8, 3, and 59 cases of WHO grades 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively. All H3 K27M-mutant tumors were grade 4. Among the H3 K27M-wildtype tumors, the distribution was 6, 8, 3, and 6 cases of grades 1 to 4, respectively. Patients were randomly assigned to training (n = 55) and test (n = 22) cohorts at a 7:3 ratio. A detailed inclusion flowchart is provided in Fig. 1.

e study was approved by the Animal and Human Ethics Committee of Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients or their legal guardians.

div.head: Imaging acquisition
div.p: Out of 77 patients, 73 underwent separate 11 C-MET PET/CT and MRI scans, while the remaining 4 underwent simultaneous brain PET/MRI. 11 C-MET PET/CT was performed on an Elite Discovery PET/CT scanner (GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA). A dose of 370-444 MBq of 11 C-MET was administered intravenously. Whole-brain PET acquisition was performed 10 min post-injection for 10 min in 3D mode. Low-dose CT was used for attenuation correction. PET images were reconstructed with VUE Point FX (18 subsets, 5 iterations, 1.0 mm Z-axis filter, matrix 192 × 192).

MRI scans were performed using three 3.0 T scanners (Discovery 750, GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA; Verio, Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany; Trio Tim, Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany). Sequences included axial T1-weighted imaging (T1WI), T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), and T2-fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images.

Simultaneous PET/MRI (n = 4) was conducted on a 3.0T time-of-flight (TOF) PET/MRI system (GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA). Ten minutes after intravenous injection of 11 C-MET (370-444 MBq), whole-brain PET and MRI were collected simultaneously in 3D mode for 20 min. e PET image was reconstructed using VUE Point FX (28 subsets, 5 iterations, 5.0 mm Z-axis filter, matrix 192 × 192).
e brain MRI sequences included T1WI, T2WI, and FLAIR. Detailed scan parameters are provided in Supplementary Table

div.head: Image analysis and tumor segmentation
div.p: For PET/CT, tumor was semi-automatically segmented using PETVCAR software (Advantage Workstation 4.6; GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA). However, for PET/MRI, LIFEx software (version 6.20; www.lifexsoft. org) was used due to software compatibility constraints. Both platforms applied the same segmentation protocol. First, the background mean standardized uptake value (SUVmean) was measured in a crescent region of interest (ROI) including both gray and white matter in the right frontal lobe. Hypermetabolic tumor regions were delineated using a threshold of 1.3 × background SUVmean [22]. If necessary, manual adjustments excluded adjacent non-tumor structures. PET metrics included maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), SUVmean, peak standardized uptake value (SUVpeak), metabolic tumour volume (MTV, expressed in milliliters), and total lesion methionine uptake (TLMU, expressed in grams) within the ROI were recorded. e tumor-to-background ratio (TBR) was calculated by dividing the SUVmax, SUVmean, and SUVpeak of the tumor by the background SUVmean.
For MRI images, tumor ROIs were manually segmented on T2WI using ITK-SNAP (version 4.0; h t t p s : / / w w w . i t k s n a p . o r g / ) , covering the tumor and peritumoral region.
e methods of tumor segmentation are illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 1. Tumor location (midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata) and growth pattern (intrinsic vs. exophytic) were recorded.

Segmentations were performed by an experienced nuclear medicine physician (8 years) and reviewed by a senior nuclear medicine physician (> 15 years). To evaluate segmentation-related feature stability, the same rater repeated PET and MRI segmentations after 6 months in a random subset of 20 patients (intra-observer test-retest). For each feature, we calculated the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and excluded features with ICC < 0.80.

div.head: Radiomics features extraction
div.p: We initially converted 11 C-MET PET images to SUV maps by normalization by injected dose and patient weight. e T1WI and FLAIR images were coregistered and resliced to the native space of T2WI images using normalized mutual information as objective function, and a 4th degree-B spline interpolation method. is procedure was performed using the SPM software package (version 12.0, h t t p : / / w w w . fi l . i o n . u c l . a c . u k / s p m /) implemented in MATLAB 2016a (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA).

e Feature Analysis Explorer (FAE version 0.3.6, h t t p s : / / g i t h u b . c o m / s a l a n 6 6 8 / F A E) software was used to extract radiomics features from SUV maps and MRI images across the entire cohort. Images were resampled to 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 mm 3 and discretized with a fixed bin width of 0.5 for SUV maps and 25 for MRI. e extracted radiomics features adhered to Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI) guidelines, including shape-based feature (n = 14), first-order feature (n = 18), gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) (n = 24), graylevel dependence matrix (GLDM) (n = 14), gray-level run length matrix (GLRLM) (n = 16), gray-level size zone matrix (GLSZM) (n = 16), and neighborhood gray tone difference matrix (NGTDM) (n = 5).

div.head: Radiomics features selection and model construction
div.p: e ComBat harmonization was fit on the training cohort and the learned parameters were applied to the test cohort to enhance the consistency of radiomic features from different scanning equipment [23]. Subsequently, the training cohort was used to construct the clinical model, radiomics model, and clinical-radiomics integrated model. A ten-fold cross-validation within the training cohort was employed to improve generalizability. Finally, the performance of three models was evaluated and compared in the test cohort.

Clinical variables, including age, gender, tumor location, growth pattern, TBRmax, TBRmean, TBRpeak, MTV, and TLMU, were evaluated. Variables with significant group differences were used to construct a clinical model using an XGBoost classifier.
Radiomics models were developed separately for PET, MRI, and PET-MRI combined features.

en, the importance of each radiomics feature for prediction was obtained and ranked with the XGBoost algorithm. To achieve the higher accuracy while maintaining the least number of features possible, the top 10 predictive features were selected to construct each model using the XGBoost classifier [24].

Based on the area under the curve (AUC) values of the radiomics models, the optimal model was selected, and its prediction probability was defined as the radiomics signature. Subsequently, a clinical-radiomics integrated model was developed by incorporating clinical features with the radiomic signature using the XGBoost classifier.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: Statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS statistics software (version 28.0) and R language software (version 4.2.1). Categorical variables were compared by the Chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. e Shapiro-Wilk test was performed to assess the normality of continuous variables.

e Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally distributed continuous variables, which were expressed as median (interquartile range). e independent sample t test was used for normally distributed continuous variables, which were recorded as ‾ x ± s.

e receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the area under the curves (AUCs) were used to evaluate the predictive efficacy of the clinical, radiomics, and clinical-radiomics integrated model. Differences in the AUC values between each model were compared using DeLong's test. e model's calibration was assessed using calibration curves to evaluate its goodness-of-fit, while decision curve analysis (DCA) was employed to determine its clinical utility. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

div.head: Clinical model performance
div.p: Among the 77 patients, 53 (68.8%) had H3 K27M-mutant tumors, and 24 (31.2%) had wildtype tumors. Patients with H3 K27M-mutant tumor were significantly younger and had shorter symptom durations than those with H3 K27M-wildtype tumor (P < 0.05). Tumors harboring the H3 K27M mutation were more frequently located in the pons and exhibited an intrinsic growth pattern (P < 0.05).

e H3 K27M-mutant tumors exhibited significantly lower TBRmax, TBRmean, and TBRpeak values than wildtype tumors (P < 0.05). No significant differences were observed in gender distribution, MTV, or TLMU between groups (P > 0.05) (Table 1). Using these significant variables, the clinical model achieved AUCs of 0.795 (95% CI: 0.661-0.891) and 0.790 (95% CI: 0.566-0.932) in the training and test cohorts, respectively. Representative 11 C-MET PET and MRI images of H3 K27M-mutant and wildtype BSGs are shown in Fig. 2.

div.head: Radiomics model performance
div.p: A total of 107 radiomics features were extracted from the PET images, and 321 from the MRI images. Based on intra-observer reproducibility, 17 PET and 38 MRI features with ICC < 0.80 were excluded, leaving 90 PET and 283 MRI features for model development.

In the PET radiomics model, the first-order feature (entropy) was identified as the most important predictor (Fig. 3A). Entropy values were significantly lower in H3K27M-mutant tumors in the test cohort (P = 0.002), although no significant difference was observed in the training cohort (P = 0.167) (Supplementary Fig. 2A-B).
is model achieved AUCs of 0.820 (95% CI: 0.692-0.911) and 0.810 (95% CI: 0.587-0.943) in the training and test cohorts, respectively.
In the MRI radiomics model, five features were derived from the T1WI, four from the T2WI, and one from the FLAIR sequence.

e most important feature was the shape-based maximum 2D diameter from T2WI (Fig. 3B). e H3 K27M-mutant group exhibited significantly larger diameters in the training cohort (P < 0.001), but not in the test cohort (P = 0.100) (Supplementary Fig. 2C-D). is model achieved AUCs of 0.825 (95% CI: 0.698-0.915) in the training cohort and 0.829 (95% CI: 0.609-0.954) in the test cohort.

In the combined PET-MRI model, one feature was derived from PET images, two from T1WI, six from T2WI, and one from FLAIR images. PET-based entropy remained the most important predictor (Fig. 3C). e model achieved AUCs of 0.876 (95% CI: 0.758-0.950) in the training cohort and 0.848 (95% CI: 0.632-0.963) in the test cohort. Comparative ROC curves of the individual PET, individual MRI, and combined PET-MRI models are shown in Fig. 4. Although the combined model numerically outperformed the PET and MRI-only models, the AUC differences were not statistically significant in either the training cohort (P > 0.05) or the test cohort

div.head: Clinical-radiomics integrated model
div.p: Based on its superior performance, the PET-MRI radiomics signature was integrated with clinical features to develop a clinical-radiomics model. It yielded the best overall performance, with AUCs of 0.886 (95% CI: 0.770-0.956) in the training cohort and 0.876 (95% CI: 0.666-0.976) in the test cohort. Feature importance analysis indicated that radiomics features contributed more substantially than clinical features. Among the clinical variables evaluated, location-pons, TBRmax, age, and disease duration exhibited relatively greater importance compared to other clinical factors (Fig. 3D).

div.head: Model comparison and validation
div.p: Although the integrated model achieved the highest AUC, DeLong's test showed no significant differences compared with the PET-MRI radiomics or clinical models (training cohort: P = 0.240 and 0.871; test cohort: P = 0.522 and 0.847, respectively). e diagnostic accuracy of the integrated model was 80.0% in the training cohort and 81.8% in the test cohort. ROC curves and diagnostic metrics are shown in Fig. 5; Table 2.

Calibration curve analysis demonstrated that the biascorrected curves of the PET-MRI and integrated model were close to the ideal line in both training and test cohorts, indicating good fit. DCA further confirmed superior clinical utility for the PET-MRI and integrated models over the clinical model alone. Calibration and decision curves are presented in Fig. 6.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: H3 K27M mutation represents the most common molecular alteration in BSGs, frequently associated with highgrade histology, aggressive clinical behavior, and poor prognosis [3,16,25]. Accurate preoperative identification of H3 K27M status is therefore critical for personalized treatment planning and predicting outcomes [26]. Our study demonstrated that radiomics models based on 11 C-MET PET and MRI can non-invasively predict H3 K27M mutation status in BSGs with favorable performance. Specifically, both PET-only and MRI-only radiomics models achieved comparable predictive performance. Notably, combining PET and MRI features further improved model accuracy, and integrating clinical variables yielded the highest predictive performance. ese findings validate the value of 11 C-MET PET in molecular prediction and support the clinical potential of a PET-MRI multimodal radiomics strategy.

We initially identified clinical characteristics correlated with H3 K27M mutation status. Additionally, we observed 11 C-MET PET semi-quantitative parameters, including TBRmax, TBRmean, and TBRpeak, were significantly lower in H3 K27M-mutant tumors.
is contrasts with a previous study by Zhao et al., which reported slightly higher uptake in the H3 K27M-mutant DIPGs, though without statistical significance [14].

is discrepancy may stem from differences in tumor location and histologic heterogeneity across studies. In this study, we also included gliomas located in the midbrain and medulla oblongata, in addition to DIPG. Different results may occur for different disease profiles.
We selected the XGBoost algorithm for constructing the radiomics model.

is aligns with a previous study performed by Kandemirli et al. [27], who successfully predicted H3 K27M mutation status in diffuse midline gliomas using XGBoost-based MRI radiomics analysis. XGBoost show superior classification performance and capability to handle multicollinearity and missing values compared to other algorithms. For example, some previous studies report that this algorithm demonstrates superior performance in classification tasks to Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, and Random Forest algorithms [28,29]. Additionally, XGBoost facilitates the quantitative assessment of feature importance, allowing for an interpretable evaluation of the predictive contributions of individual features [30]. predicting H3 K27M status in BSGs. Studies using PET radiomics for molecular diagnostics are relatively rare, primarily due to the limited availability of PET tracers, high costs, and technical complexity involved in standardizing PET radiomics pipelines. However, PET radiomics may better capture metabolic heterogeneity and reflect underlying tumor biology more directly than MRI, warranting further research.

Among the PET-derived features, entropy, a first-order feature, was identified as the most important. Entropy quantifies intensity randomness and is widely used as a radiomic surrogate of intratumoral heterogeneity [31]. In this study, entropy was higher in the H3 K27M-wildtype group, implying that wildtype tumors may harbor more intratumoral heterogeneity, potentially linked to resistance mechanisms and poorer response to therapy. In diffuse gliomas, cellular and genetic heterogeneity fuels therapy resistance and relapse, providing a biologic rationale for the adverse association we observed [32]. Consistent with this, amino-acid PET heterogeneity has been established as a prognostic indicator in gliomas. is is evidenced by studies showing that textural features of 18 F-FET PET uptake predict tumor grade and survival in high-grade gliomas [33] and that preoperative 11 C-MET PET texture analysis predicts postsurgical survival [34].

For the MRI model, the most important feature was the maximum 2D diameter from T2WI, which was larger in H3 K27M-mutant tumors. is finding aligns with a previous study [35] and may reflect the diffuse and expansive nature of H3 K27M-mutant gliomas, particularly those located in the pons.

Previous literature suggests that PET/MRI multimodal radiomics can enhance diagnostic performance over monomodal approaches [36,37]. In our study, the combined PET-MRI radiomics model numerically outperformed individual modalities, with AUCs of 0.876 and 0.848 in the training and test cohorts, respectively. is suggests that the integration of metabolic and structural imaging captures complementary information, enhancing predictive robustness.
To further improve predictive performance, we developed a clinical-radiomics integrated model by combining clinical variables with the PET-MRI radiomics signature.

is model yielded AUCs of 0.886 and 0.876, the highest among all models. DCA demonstrated improved net clinical benefit, supporting its potential utility in decision-making. ese findings align with those of Pan et al., who demonstrated that combining clinical parameters with MRI radiomics features outperformed either alone for predicting H3 K27M mutation status [16]. Our results also emphasize that clinical variables, such as location, growth pattern, and metabolic parameters, should not be neglected in radiomics-based modelling for BSGs.

is study has several limitations. Firstly, the study is a single-center, retrospective study with a relatively small sample size and without an external validation cohort. Although imaging was performed on multiple scanners, all data were acquired at Beijing Tiantan Hospital; accordingly, the dataset is not multicentric. Multiscanner heterogeneity may provide some robustness to hardware variability, but it does not capture inter-center differences in patient spectrum, referral patterns, acquisition and reconstruction protocols, or clinical practice, and thus limits external validity. Prospective, large-scale, multicenter studies with independent external validation cohorts are needed to confirm and refine the model. Secondly, since the PETVCAR software is exclusively designed for ROI segmentation on PET/CT images, we utilized the LIFEx software for ROI segmentation on PET images obtained from PET/MRI. e two different software tools may result in variations in the delineated ROI, due to distinct segmentation algorithms and contour processing methods. However, consistent segmentation thresholds and the small number of PET/MRI (n = 4) minimized this impact on the overall results.

irdly, most PET and MRI images were acquired at different time points and scanners. is might result in imperfect spatial alignment between two modalities. Further work should include more cases with simultaneous PET/MRI acquisition to ensure optimal co-registration and consistency of features. Finally, while all H3 K27M-mutant gliomas were grade 4 in our cohort, the H3 K27M-wildtype group comprised both low-and high-grade tumors, which are known to exhibit distinct pathological and biological behaviors. Consequently, histologic heterogeneity could affect the robustness of the results. To address this, in future work, we will conduct a grade-stratified analysis in an expanded cohort to systematically explore the impact of tumor heterogeneity on model performance.

In conclusion, this study provides evidence that radiomics analysis of 11 C-MET PET and MRI can noninvasively and accurately predict H3 K27M mutation status in BSGs. e integration of clinical features with radiomics further improves predictive performance.

ese findings support the implementation of multimodal radiomics as a promising tool for personalized diagnosis and treatment planning in brainstem gliomas. To solidify these preliminary findings, future research should include large-scale, multicenter cohorts to validate the practical application of this approach in clinical settings.
